identity.real_world_identity_notes: GT1 car built for Le Mans around a twin-turbo 3.5 litre V8, with the road-going homologation special sharing its name. Power reaches the rear wheels through an Xtrac six-speed sequential gearbox worked by a short-throw gear lever, which matches the sequential stick seen in the cockpit rather than paddles.

wheel_rim.notes: No exact Nissan cockpit drawing or reliable source was found for rim geometry or wheel-mounted shift lights.

notes: Simulator behavior was directly observed in a guided drive with automatic clutch and shifting disabled.
The clutch is required to move off, and the gear lever is a sequential stick rather than paddles.

In AMS2, no throttle lift is required on upshifts because a full-throttle clutchless upshift was accepted with automatic cut detected. No automatic blip was detected, so that implementation requires the driver to supply the downshift blip; the real car's blip technique remains unknown.
'Nissan R390 GT1 - Low Downforce' inherits these verified base controls as an approved aero-package assumption and was not separately live-tested.

RSS's first-party pack documentation and installed metadata identify the exact fingerprinted implementation as the primarily-1998 long-tail, 3,495 cc twin-turbo V8 car. NISMO independently gives that same combination only to the 1998 R390 GT1 and records its sequential transmission. Six sequential-stick gears, clutch-required move-off, automatic cut/blip, and cockpit wheel equipment were directly observed.

claims.basis: NISMO establishes the 1998 long-tail's Nissan-built sequential transmission but gives no driver rev-match or ECU automatic-blip procedure. Sequential construction cannot settle either field.
NISMO's exact history contains no cockpit drawing or specification that establishes rim geometry or wheel-mounted shift lights.
A registered secondary source establishes the 1998 GT1 identity and its Xtrac sequential gearbox, and the exact simulator identity was observed live.
The source specifies an Xtrac six-speed sequential operated by a short-throw lever, and the live drive confirmed six gears through a sequential stick.
Directly observed during the guided drive: move-off, shift clutch use, automatic cut and blip, and the cockpit rim.
The drive accepted a full-throttle clutchless upshift with automatic cut, so no lift is required, and detected no automatic blip on downshifts, so the driver supplies the rev-matching blip.

RSS Classic Endurance Pack 1 readme, PDF/printed page 3, says the Nisumo R39 was built for 1997 and 1998, depicts the long-tail used primarily in 1998, and uses a 3,495 cc twin-turbo V8. NISMO's own history says the 1998 Nissan R390 GT1 became a long-tail and changed to a Nissan-built sequential transmission. The year, body revision, displacement, engine layout, aspiration, category and fictionalized model token converge on the existing 1998 R390 GT1 record rather than a neighboring Nissan prototype.
